Do indefinido ao imperfecto de subjuntiv: From the indefinido to the imperfecto de subjuntivo
PASSO 1: o «imperfecto de subjuntivo» é: STEP 1: the «imperfecto de subjuntivo» is the past subjunctive. You use it when the main verb is in the past and calls for the subjunctive: «Quiero que vengas» (I want you to come) becomes «Quería que vinieras» (I wanted you to come). English keeps "you to come" in both; Spanish shifts the subjunctive to the past. STEP 2: English has one survivor of this form: "WERE" in "If I were you", "I wish it were Friday", "as if he were the boss". Spanish «fuera» is exactly that "were" — and Spanish has it for every verb. STEP 3: to form it, start from the «ellos» form of the pretérito indefinido: «hablaron», «comieron», «vivieron». STEP 4: drop the final «-ron»: «habla-», «comie-», «vivie-». STEP 5: add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran: «hablara, hablaras, hablara, habláramos, hablarais, hablaran». Only the «nosotros» form has a written accent, on the vowel before the ending: «habláramos», «comiéramos», «viviéramos». STEP 6: irregular verbs have no new rule. The stem comes from the indefinido: «tuvieron» gives «tuviera», «fueron» gives «fuera», «dijeron» gives «dijera». If you know the «ellos» indefinido, you know this form. STEP 7: there's a second set, in -se: «hablase, hablases, hablase, hablásemos, hablaseis, hablasen». The meaning is the same. In Spain both are used (-ra more in speech); in Latin America -ra dominates. In this lesson the sentences use -ra, and the tables show both. STEP 8: one form covers «yo» and «él»: «Quería que yo tuviera» and «Quería que él tuviera». Use the pronoun when you need to make clear who does it.

Quando o verbo principal está no passado: When the main verb is in the past
PASSO 1: a regra de concordância é simpl: STEP 1: the agreement rule is simple. A main verb in the present (or future) takes the present subjunctive; a main verb in the past takes the imperfecto de subjuntivo. «Me pide que espere» (She asks me to wait) becomes «Me pidió que esperara» (She asked me to wait). STEP 2: this works for the same ideas you saw in the present: requests and advice («pedir, aconsejar, recomendar, permitir, prohibir»), wishes («querer, esperar»), doubt and denial («dudar, no creer»), emotion («me alegró que, me sorprendió que») and judgement («era importante que, era mejor que»). STEP 3: with the pretérito perfecto («he pedido», «ha dicho») you're still thinking in the present, so you use the present subjunctive: «Me ha pedido que vaya». With the indefinido and the imperfecto, use the imperfecto de subjuntivo. STEP 4: «ojalá» with the imperfecto de subjuntivo expresses a difficult or unreal wish about now — exactly like English "I wish" + past: «Ojalá tuviera más tiempo» (I wish I HAD more time — but I don't). With the present, the wish is possible: «Ojalá tengas suerte» (I hope you're lucky). STEP 5: «como si» (as if) always takes the imperfecto de subjuntivo when it compares with something unreal — English "as if he WERE": «Habla como si fuera mi jefe» (but he isn't). STEP 6: in polite requests, «quisiera» is softer than «quiero», like English "I would like": «Quisiera reservar una mesa». You've used it since lesson 29; now you know where it comes from: it's the imperfecto de subjuntivo of «querer». STEP 7: with «dudar» and «no creer» in the past, the subjunctive stays: «No creía que fuera verdad» (I didn't think it was true). «Creía que era verdad» (an affirmation) takes the indicative.

Para que, antes de que, sin que e relati: Para que, antes de que, sin que and relative clauses
PASSO 1: as conjunções que você aprendeu: STEP 1: the conjunctions from lesson 44 («para que», «antes de que», «sin que») take the subjunctive. If the main verb is in the past, the subjunctive moves to the imperfecto: «Te llamé para que vinieras» (I called you so that you would come). English "so that you WOULD come" — but never «vendrías» here. STEP 2: «antes de que» always takes the subjunctive, even in the past: «Salimos antes de que lloviera» (We left before it rained). STEP 3: «sin que» is only used when the subjects are different: «Se fue sin que nadie lo viera» (He left without anyone seeing him). With the same subject, use «sin» + infinitive: «Se fue sin despedirse» (without saying goodbye). STEP 4: when what you're looking for is unknown or may not exist, the relative clause takes the subjunctive: «Buscaba un piso que tuviera terraza» (I was looking for a flat that had a terrace — any flat, if one existed). If the flat is a specific one, use the indicative: «Encontré un piso que tenía terraza». STEP 5: «cuando» for a past habit takes the indicative: «Cuando era niño, jugaba en la calle». The subjunctive only appears for something that hadn't happened yet from the point of view of the past: «Dijo que me llamaría cuando llegara» (He said he'd call me when he arrived).
